source_evidence.anchor: Section 2.4 definition of the Erdős–Rényi model and the display “(n − 1)p =: d”
source_evidence.observation: E1: G(n,p) has n vertices, every pair of distinct vertices is connected independently with probability p, vertex degree counts incident edges, and every vertex has expected degree d=(n−1)p.
E2: All exercises in this series are interpreted while n grows to infinity, and p is explicitly allowed to depend on n.

source_evidence.anchor: Exercise 2.4.4, “Sparse graphs are not almost regular”
source_evidence.observation: E3: For G distributed as G(n,p) with expected degree d=o(log n), the requested event is that G has a vertex with degree exactly 10d, and the event is to hold with high probability, with 0.9 given as a concrete example.

source_evidence.anchor: Footnote 3 attached to the word “degree” in Exercise 2.4.4
source_evidence.observation: E4: The source assumes 10d is an integer and says that the factor 10 is not special and may be replaced by another constant.
E5: The hint notes that the ordinary degrees d_i are dependent, suggests replacing them by independent quantities d'_i by counting only some vertices, and then invokes Poisson approximation (2.9).
E6: For X distributed as Pois(λ), equation (2.9) approximates the point mass P{X=k} by (1/sqrt(2πk)) e^(−λ)(eλ/k)^k using Stirling’s formula.

binders: [E1,E2] A graph size n, taking positive integer values and tending to infinity.
[E1,E2] A connection probability p=p(n), which may vary with n and has the probability-valued range implicit in G(n,p).
[E1,E3] A random graph G sampled from the Erdős–Rényi distribution G(n,p).
[E1] The common expected vertex degree d=(n−1)p.
hypotheses: [E2,E3] The asymptotic sparsity condition is d=o(log n) as n tends to infinity.
[E4] The threshold 10d is assumed to be an integer.
conclusions: [E2,E3] As n tends to infinity, with high probability—0.9 being explicitly offered as a concrete level—there exists a vertex v of G whose degree equals 10d.
[E3,E4] The source asks for equality deg_G(v)=10d, not merely deg_G(v)≥10d; the integrality footnote is attached precisely to this value.
definitions_and_conventions: [E1] G(n,p) is formed by independently connecting each pair of distinct vertices with probability p.
[E1] The degree of a vertex is its number of incident edges.
[E1] The symbol d denotes the common expected degree (n−1)p, not an independently chosen threshold.
[E6] The referenced Poisson approximation is a point-mass estimate for P{X=k}, consistent with seeking a vertex of one exact degree.
implicit_context: [E2] The condition d=o(log n) and the probability assertion belong to an asymptotic family of random graphs rather than to a single fixed n.
[E2] No assumption that p is constant in n may be imported.
[E7] Exact occurrence of degree 10d supplies the advertised lower bound on the maximum degree, but that maximum-degree inequality is a consequence rather than the exercise’s literal target.

details: [E2,E3] The graph parameters vary with n, the little-o condition constrains that variation, and the existence event is evaluated under the law of G(n,p).
[E3] The existential quantifier ranges over the n vertices inside the random event.
[E3] The grammatical claim is that some vertex has degree 10d exactly.
[E4] Requiring 10d to be integral supports the exact-value reading.
[E5,E6] The suggested point-mass Poisson approximation also supports the exact-value reading.
[E3] The source uses the phrase “with high probability” and parenthetically gives 0.9 as an acceptable concrete probability.
[E2] Because n tends to infinity, any fixed 0.9 formulation necessarily concerns sufficiently large n.
[E5] Vertex degrees d_i are explicitly recognized as dependent.
[E5] Independence of auxiliary restricted degrees d'_i and Poisson approximation are proof suggestions, not additional hypotheses or conclusions.
[E4] The source separately assumes the resulting real-valued expected-degree multiple 10d is an integer.

undebatable_constraints: [E1] The expected-degree parameter must remain tied to d=(n−1)p.
[E2,E3] The asymptotic hypothesis is little-o, d=o(log n), not merely an unspecified upper bound of order log n.
[E2] The connection probability may depend on n.
[E3] The event is existential: at least one vertex must have the stated degree.
[E3,E4,E5,E6] The stated degree is exactly 10d; replacing equality by only a lower-tail inequality changes the literal claim.
[E4] Integrality of 10d is an inherited explicit assumption and cannot be silently dropped without supplying a rounding convention.
[E3] The probability guarantee must retain the source’s high-probability language and its explicit allowance of 0.9 as a concrete target.
[E5] The independence construction and Poisson approximation are proof guidance and must not be promoted into assumptions on G.

ambiguities.issue: The source does not formally define “with high probability” in this passage.

ambiguities.impact: A formal target may encode eventual probability at least 0.9, or may encode convergence of the event probability to 1. The former is the explicit concrete level; the latter is the conventional stronger asymptotic reading of the phrase.

ambiguities.impact: A formalization must either restrict the asymptotic family to indices satisfying 10d∈ℤ or introduce an explicitly justified rounding convention; the source itself supplies no rounding rule.

contract_plain_english: [E1–E4] Consider an asymptotic Erdős–Rényi family G(n,p(n)), where every vertex has expected degree d=(n−1)p and d/log n tends to zero. Assuming 10d is an integer, the source asks one to show that, for large n, with high probability—0.9 is explicitly acceptable—there is some vertex whose degree is exactly 10d. [E5,E6] The suggested proof avoids the dependence among ordinary vertex degrees by counting a restricted independent family and uses a Poisson point-mass approximation.
